lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you planned an argument with a map. What sits at the top? (The claim: the point you want the reader to accept.) Today: argue like a pro, with counterclaims, sources and a strong ending.

A claim is the position you argue. A counterclaim is the strongest view against it. Name it fairly (“Some argue that…”), then answer it with a rebuttal (“However, …”). Answering the other side makes you more convincing.

picture.claim: Our school should start a garden.
picture.counter: Some say it takes too much time.
picture.rebuttal: A rota needs only an hour a week.

lesson.text: Signal words show whose view is whose. For the other side: “Some argue”, “Admittedly”, “It is true that”. For your answer: “However”, “Yet”, “Even so”. To add a reason: “Furthermore”.

Back your reasons with evidence from credible sources. Ask: who wrote it, and what do they know? Is it recent? Could they gain from what they say? Can another good source confirm it? Then name the source.
Logical reasoning links evidence to the claim. Avoid tricks: “everyone does it” is not a reason, and attacking a person instead of their point proves nothing.
Write in a formal style: no slang, precise words and a calm tone. “Loads of kids hate it” becomes “Many pupils are unhappy with it.”
End with a strong conclusion. Say your claim again in new words and sum up your best reason. Show the counterclaim is answered. Finish with a call to action, or a thought that stays.

Try it in the world: in Talk & Deal in the LIFE tab, pitch your bread cart to three investors. When one doubts you, answer the way a rebuttal answers a counterclaim: fairly, with evidence. Next: explain complex ideas.

choices: the strongest view against your claim
a fact that backs you up
exercises.explain: A counterclaim is the strongest view against yours; a strong argument names it fairly and answers it.

exercises.prompt: Sort the signal words: bringing in the other side, or answering it?
exercises.hint: Which words let the other view in, and which push back?
exercises.explain: “Some argue”, “Admittedly” and “It is true that” bring in the other side; “However”, “Yet” and “Even so” answer it.

exercises.prompt: Answering a counterclaim makes an argument weaker.
exercises.hint: Does a reader trust someone who ignores the other side?
exercises.explain: False: answering it shows you have thought the issue through, which makes you more convincing.

exercises.prompt: Which source is most credible for how much rain fell last year?
exercises.hint: Who measures rain carefully and gains nothing from the answer?
exercises.explain: The national weather service measures rainfall carefully and has nothing to sell; the others may guess or gain.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of an argument to its job.
exercises.hint: Think about the order an argument goes in.
exercises.explain: The claim is what you argue; the counterclaim is the view against it; the rebuttal answers it; the conclusion ends strongly.

exercises.prompt: Claim: our town needs more trees. Which is the best rebuttal to this counterclaim?
choices: Yet trees cut cooling costs on hot days.
Money is not important at all.
exercises.hint: A rebuttal answers the doubt with a reason or evidence.
exercises.explain: It answers the worry about money with a reason: trees save money by cooling streets. The others give no reason.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is written in a formal style?
choices: Many residents would welcome more trees.
Trees are well good, everyone loves them.
You'd be mad not to want trees!
exercises.hint: Look for calm, precise words with no slang.
exercises.explain: “Many residents would welcome more trees” is calm and exact; the others use slang or exaggerate.

exercises.prompt: Put the argument's paragraphs in a strong order.
items: Conclude with a call to action
exercises.hint: Set out your case before you bring in the other side.
exercises.explain: The claim, then reasons and evidence, then the counterclaim, your rebuttal, and a conclusion with a call to action.

exercises.prompt: Which is a weak reason, not logical reasoning?
choices: A study found it saves water.
It costs less over ten years.
exercises.hint: Which one gives no evidence, only a crowd?
exercises.explain: “Everyone else is doing it” gives no evidence about whether it is good: it is a crowd, not a reason.

exercises.prompt: Attacking the person who disagrees is a good way to answer a counterclaim.
exercises.hint: Does it say anything about their point?
exercises.explain: False: attacking a person proves nothing about their point; a rebuttal answers the point with reasons.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: claim, counterclaim or rebuttal?
items: Our park needs a water fountain.
Even so, they would fit by the gate.
However, it would cut plastic bottle waste.
Bike racks would help our school.
Some say fountains cost a lot to run.
exercises.hint: Signal words help: “Some say” and “Admittedly” bring in the other side; “However” and “Even so” answer it.
exercises.explain: The claims are the fountain and the bike racks. “Some say” and “Admittedly” start counterclaims; “However” and “Even so” start rebuttals.

exercises.prompt: Which is the strongest conclusion for an argument that the library should open on Saturdays?
choices: Open on Saturdays, and the whole town gains.
That is all I have to say.
exercises.hint: A strong ending says the claim again and calls for action.
exercises.explain: It says the claim again in new words and calls for action; the others add nothing or wander off the point.

exercises.prompt: Order the sentences into a strong conclusion.
items: Let us start digging this spring.
So a school garden is worth the effort.
A rota answers the worry about time.
Pupils would learn where food comes from.
exercises.hint: Say the claim again, then the best reason, then answer the doubt, then call for action.
exercises.explain: First the claim in new words: a garden is worth it. Then the best reason: pupils learn about food. Then the counterclaim answered: a rota solves the time problem. Last, the call to action.

exercises.prompt: Your source for a claim about gardening is a website that sells garden tools. What is the problem?
choices: it may gain from what it claims
exercises.hint: Ask: could the writer gain from what they say?
exercises.explain: A seller may gain if you believe it. Check the claim in a source with nothing to sell, such as a university or a gardening society, before you use it as evidence.

exercises.prompt: A counterclaim should be stated fairly, in its strongest form.
exercises.hint: What happens if you answer only a weak version of the other side?
exercises.explain: True: rebutting the strongest version convinces readers; answering a weak one looks like dodging the issue.

exercises.prompt: Match each signal word to its job.
exercises.hint: Two are about the other side, one adds, and one ends.
exercises.explain: “Admittedly” brings in the other side and “However” answers it; “Furthermore” adds a reason; “Therefore” draws a conclusion.
